title: Obsolete evidence reduced correct answers even when the latest fact was present
summary: In a paired experiment on 74 questions, replacing one unrelated statement with an obsolete version of the answer reduced accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5-7B and to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B. The newest statement remained present in both conditions.
organization: Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg; University of Kerala; Technical University of Munich

source_review.scope: Paired design, frozen conditions, Table 16 and limitations

evidence.tested: The experiment held the four-statement evidence size and prompt fixed. Under the official normalized-substring metric, all 50 harmful flips across the two models were classified as using outdated information. A later manual audit found mixed latest/stale strings in two Qwen2.5 outputs; a stricter score gave 98.6% versus 43.2%, retaining the same paired discordance.
evidence.unknown: The same 74 questions informed prompt development, so this is a within-cohort contrast and generalization remains open. The study concerns synthetic single-hop updates and two Qwen models. Obsolete values often match familiar real-world knowledge while the synthetic newest statements contradict it; the experiment does not isolate temporal obsolescence from pretrained-prior conflict. Output scoring and the measured behavioral effect do not establish attention or other internal mechanisms.
evidence.ai_role: The two learned language models composed answers from matched evidence sets, enabling a direct test of which retrieved version they used.
